newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl government in crisis meeting on budget, gold.
newsitem.headline: Kohl government in crisis meeting on budget, gold.

text.p: German government leaders held a crisis meeting at Chancellor Helmut Kohl's office on Sunday to try to plug holes in the budget and defuse an explosive row over a plan to revalue Bundesbank gold and currency reserves.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel and other leaders of Kohl's centre-right government drove quickly past journalists into the chancellery. None of them stopped to answer questions.

Waigel has to cope with 15 billion marks ($8.8 billion) less in tax income than originally projected in the 1998 budget and spending is likely to be higher than forecast because of record post-war unemployment.
He declined to comment on Saturday on reports that he would use the meeting to propose a rise in fuel tax or a postponement of a planned reduction of an income tax surcharge.

Kohl's coalition partners, the liberal Free Democrats (FDP), have repeatedly said they will not approve tax increases to plug holes in the budget, indicating that that the future of the coalition could be at stake if Waigel insists on tax rises.
Officials said Sunday's meeting was not likely to produce any final decisions.

A battle between the government and the Bundesbank over Waigel's plan to revalue gold and currency reserves this year has dominated German political debate over the past few days and looked certain to be discussed at some stage.
Hans Tietmeyer, the head of the powerful central bank, denied a report in Der Spiegel magazine that he had proposed a delay in the 1999 start date for Europe's single currency.
He insisted he was committed to the European Union's Maastricht Treaty, which lays down the timetable and criteria for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
But he reiterated the Bundesbank's opposition to revaluing the bank's reserves and called on the government to take proper note of its objections.
"Reports of suggestions by the Bundesbank or its president in favour of a postponement of the start of the monetary union are not accurate," he said in a statement.
"The Deutsche Bundesbank naturally stands by the Maastricht Treaty. The bank has already been working intensively for a long time on the preparation of monetary union with a stable euro."
Spiegel had quoted Tietmeyer as breaking one of Kohl's political taboos by asking if Bonn and Paris could delay the start of the single currency.

Some members of Kohl's coalition also voiced opposition to Waigel's revaluation plan, raising the possibility that the veteran chancellor might not be able to muster a majority to push the controversial measure through parliament.
The related row over how to fill shortfalls in government finances, where Waigel is on a collision course with the Free Democrat, added to Kohl's woes.

The Bundesbank has condemned the gold plan as an attack on its fabled independence, but Waigel and other coalition leaders, turning the row into a battle between institutions, stressed that parliament was also an independent body.
"I expect the Bundesbank to respect the legislative independence of politics just as politics always respects the independence of the Bundesbank in monetary policy," Waigel told journalists.

His plan aims to reap 20 billion marks ($12 billion) that could partly ease the government's debt burden and help to meet the EMU entry criteria. The decision on which countries qualify for the single currency will be based on 1997 data.
Tietmeyer said the Bundesbank's main objection concerned the fact that the revaluation would boost 1997 balance sheets.
"The Bundesbank hopes that the German government and parliament will take appropriate consideration of these objections when they make their decisions," he said.
Grumbling from members of Kohl's coalition suggested that several members of parliament were indeed taking heed.
FDP budget expert Juergen Koppelin urged the government to retreat from what was shaping up to be an unprecedented clash with the central bank.
Juergen Augustinowitz, a young Christian Democrat who has already announced he will not vote for legislation opposed by the Bundesbank, said he was sure he would not be alone.
